title: Top K Frequent Elements
directAnswer: Count every value with a hash map, then select the k most frequent. The interview-grade answer is a min-heap of size k keyed by frequency: push (count, value) and pop whenever the heap exceeds k, leaving the k largest — O(n log k) time. The strongest answer is bucket sort: index values by their frequency (1..n) and read from the high-frequency end, giving true O(n) time.

remember.pattern: Frequency map + size-k heap (or bucket sort)
rules: Use a **min-heap of size k**, not a max-heap of size n — you only ever need to keep the k best.
Pop when the heap **exceeds** k, so the smallest frequency falls out and the k largest survive.
If the interviewer wants strict O(n), pivot to **bucket sort** — frequencies are bounded by n, so they index cleanly into n+1 buckets.
k is guaranteed `1 ≤ k ≤ number of distinct elements`, so the answer is always well-defined — no need to handle k > distinct.
Full sort of (value, count) pairs is O(n log n) — fine to mention, but the heap (O(n log k)) and bucket sort (O(n)) both beat it.
whenToUse: 'Top K', 'K most frequent', 'K largest/smallest' over a collection
You need a partial ordering of the K best, not a full sort
Streaming data where K stays small relative to n
Frequencies / keys are bounded integers (then bucket sort wins)
antiSignals: k ≈ n → just sort, the heap gives no advantage
You need the elements fully sorted → sort directly
Single max/min (k = 1) → a linear scan beats a heap
Data fits a bounded range → counting / bucket sort is O(n)
remember.takeaway: Top-K is the signature heap problem: a size-k heap converts 'find the K best' from an O(n log n) sort into O(n log k). When the keys you rank are bounded (like frequencies ≤ n), bucket sort drops it to O(n). Same shape powers K Closest Points, K Largest, and Kth Largest in a Stream.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you separate 'count' from 'select', and whether you reach for a size-k heap instead of fully sorting — plus whether you know the O(n) bucket-sort upgrade.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Building a max-heap of all n elements (O(n log n)) instead of a min-heap capped at size k (O(n log k)), or sorting the whole frequency map when only the top k matter.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Name three tiers out loud — sort O(n log n), size-k heap O(n log k), bucket sort O(n) — then justify which to pick from k versus n, and mention quickselect as the O(n)-average comparison-based alternative.

problemStatement: Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return **the `k` most frequent elements**. You may return the answer in any order.
constraints: k is in the range [1, number of unique elements in nums]
The answer is guaranteed to be unique
Follow-up: your algorithm's time complexity must be better than O(n log n)
understanding: Two independent sub-tasks: (1) compute how many times each distinct value appears, and (2) pick the k values with the highest counts. The output is the values themselves (in any order), not their counts or indices.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can there be ties in frequency at the k-th boundary?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The problem guarantees the answer is unique, so the k-th cutoff is unambiguous. If ties were allowed I'd confirm whether any valid set of k is acceptable.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the output need to be sorted by frequency?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — 'any order' is allowed. That's exactly why a heap (which gives partial order) suffices over a full sort.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How large is k relative to n?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: If k is tiny vs n, a size-k heap (O(n log k)) shines. If k ≈ n, I'd just sort. Bucket sort is O(n) regardless of k.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are the values bounded?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: They fit in [-10⁴, 10⁴], but more importantly any frequency is at most n. That bound is what makes bucket sort an O(n) option.

examples.explanation: 1 appears 3 times, 2 appears twice, 3 appears once. The two most frequent are 1 and 2.
Single distinct value; it is trivially the most frequent.
4 appears 3 times, more than any other value, so the single most frequent is 4.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach

approaches.name: Min-Heap of Size K
approaches.whenToMention: The default interview answer. Lead with 'count, then keep a heap of only the k best' — emphasise the size-k cap, not just 'use a heap'.
hints: Two phases: first tally counts, then pick the top k. What structure gives O(1) counting? And what structure efficiently maintains 'the best k seen so far'?
Build a hash map value → count in O(n). Now you have at most n distinct (value, count) pairs to rank.
Push each (count, value) into a min-heap. After every push, if the heap holds more than k items, pop the smallest. The smallest is always the least frequent survivor, so the k most frequent remain.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Counting is O(n). Each of the ≤ n distinct values triggers a push and possibly a pop, each O(log k) because the heap never exceeds size k. Total O(n log k). The map plus heap are O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Solve it in two clean phases.

**Phase 1 — count.** Walk `nums` once building a hash map from value to its frequency. This is O(n) and reduces the problem to ranking at most n distinct (value, count) pairs.

**Phase 2 — keep only the k best with a min-heap.** A *min*-heap (smallest on top) is the counter-intuitive but correct choice. Push `(count, value)` for each distinct value. The instant the heap grows past k, pop the top — which is the *least* frequent element currently held. Because we only ever discard the smallest, whatever remains after processing every value is exactly the k largest by frequency.

**Why min-heap, not max-heap.** It feels natural to build a max-heap of all n elements and pop k times — but that's O(n + k log n) with an O(n) heapify, and more importantly stores all n elements. The size-k min-heap caps memory at k and makes each operation O(log k) instead of O(log n). When k ≪ n this is a real win and signals you understand 'top-K' as a bounded-heap pattern, not a sort.

**Why (count, value) ordering matters.** The heap must order by frequency, so frequency is the first tuple element (Python compares tuples lexicographically; Java needs a comparator on count). Getting the comparator backwards is the classic bug — you'd keep the k *least* frequent.
approaches.insight: A min-heap of size k is a sliding 'hall of fame': the doorman (the heap top) is always the weakest current member, so admitting a stronger candidate evicts exactly the right one. You never need to see all n elements at once — perfect for streams where n is unbounded but k is fixed.

approaches.name: Bucket Sort by Frequency (Optimal O(n))
approaches.whenToMention: Bring this up when the follow-up asks for better than O(n log n). It's the strongest answer: counts are bounded by n, so they bucket cleanly.
hints: A frequency can never exceed n (you only have n elements). What if you indexed values by their frequency directly?
Make an array of n+1 buckets. Place each value into bucket[its frequency]. Now bucket[f] lists every value occurring exactly f times.
Walk the buckets from the highest frequency downward, collecting values until you have k. No comparisons, no log factor — pure O(n).
approaches.complexityReasoning: Counting is O(n). Filling buckets visits each distinct value once — O(n). Scanning buckets high-to-low touches each bucket index and each stored value once — O(n) total. Buckets plus map are O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Exploit a hard bound: with n elements, no value can appear more than n times. So frequencies live in the small integer range `[1, n]` and can be used as array indices.

**Build the buckets.** Create `buckets[0..n]`, where `buckets[f]` is a list of all values whose frequency is exactly `f`. After counting, iterate the map once and append each value to its frequency's bucket. This is a counting-sort idea: instead of comparing frequencies, we *place* values at their frequency.

**Read from the top.** Walk `f` from `n` down to `1`. Each bucket you hit contains the next-most-frequent group of values; append them to the result until you've collected k. Because higher indices are scanned first, the most frequent come out first.

**Why this beats the heap.** There's no comparison and no logarithm anywhere — every step is a direct index or append. The total work is linear in n, which is the theoretical floor (you must at least read the input). This is the answer the follow-up is fishing for.

**Why n+1 buckets.** Frequencies range from 1 to n inclusive, so we need indices up to n. Allocating index 0 (always empty) keeps the indexing arithmetic trivial — `buckets[f]` with no offset.
approaches.insight: Bucket sort works here purely because the *key we sort on* (frequency) is bounded by n. The instant the thing you're ranking has a small bounded range, a comparison sort is overkill — counting/bucket placement turns O(n log n) into O(n). Spotting that bound is the whole trick.

Place the value at the index equal to its frequency — counting-sort placement, no comparison.

java.line: for (int f = nums.length; f >= 1 && idx < k; f--)
java.explanation: Scan from highest frequency down; stop as soon as we've gathered k values.
Guard against overshooting when a single bucket holds more values than we still need.

python.explanation: n+1 empty lists; index = frequency. Each is its own list (avoid the shared-reference bug).
Bucket the value by how often it appears — the linear-time replacement for sorting.
Walk frequencies high → low so the most frequent values come out first.
Early return the moment we have k values — no need to scan the rest.

pitfalls: Sizing buckets to max(value) instead of n — wrong axis; you bucket by FREQUENCY, which is bounded by n.
In Python, `[[]] * (n+1)` creates n+1 references to ONE list — use a comprehension so each bucket is independent.
Forgetting to stop at k — you'd over-collect when a bucket holds several values.

commonMistakes: Building a max-heap of all n elements instead of a size-k min-heap — wastes a log factor and O(n) memory.
Inverting the heap comparator so it keeps the k least frequent values.
Sorting the entire frequency map when the follow-up explicitly asks for better than O(n log n).

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Max-heap of n elements instead of size-k min-heap
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Heaping all distinct values and popping k times is O(n log n)-ish and stores everything. A size-k min-heap caps memory at k and each op at log k.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
heap = [(-f, v) for v, f in count.items()]  # all n, max-heap
heapq.heapify(heap)
return [heapq.heappop(heap)[1] for _ in range(k)]

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Reversed comparator keeps the wrong k
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If the size-k heap is ordered as a MAX-heap on frequency, every pop removes the most frequent, so you end up retaining the k LEAST frequent values.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
PriorityQueue<int[]> heap =
    new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> b[1] - a[1]); // max-heap
heap.offer(new int[]{key, freq});
if (heap.size() > k) heap.poll(); // pops the MOST frequent
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
PriorityQueue<int[]> heap =
    new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> a[1] - b[1]); // min-heap
heap.offer(new int[]{key, freq});
if (heap.size() > k) heap.poll(); // pops the LEAST frequent

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Shared bucket references in Python
commonMistakesDetailed.why: `[[]] * (n+1)` makes every index point to the SAME list, so appending to one bucket appears in all of them, corrupting the result.
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
buckets = [[] for _ in range(len(nums) + 1)]
buckets[freq].append(value)  # each bucket independent

patternNote: Top-K via size-k heap (O(n log k)) or bucket sort (O(n)). Reach for it whenever you need the K best by some key without a full sort. Same family as Kth Largest Element, K Closest Points to Origin, and Sort Characters By Frequency.
